# A Qualitative Study of Hospitals & Payers Implementing Community Doula Support

**Authors:** Christina Gebel; Elysia Larson; Heather Olden; Cara B. Safon; Tonia J. Rhone; Ndidiamaka N. Amutah-Onukagha

**Affiliations:** Department of Community Health Sciences, Boston University School of Public Health, Boston, MA 121 Canter Place Durham, NC 27712 | Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Department of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology, Harvard Medical School, 330 Brookline Ave., KS3, Boston, MA 02215 | Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health, 677 Huntington Ave. Boston, MA 02115. | Department of Health Law, Policy, and Management, Boston University School of Public Health, Boston, MA | Wright State University Boonshoft School of Medicine, 3640 Colonel Glenn Hwy, Fairborn, OH 45324 | Department of Public Health and Community Medicine, Tufts University School of Medicine, 200 Harrison Ave, Boston, MA 02111

## Abstract

The impact of doula care on birth outcomes is well-established; however, doula support remains underutilized. Identifying barriers and facilitators to implementation is integral as the demand for doula care increases. The primary objective of this study was to examine doula program implementation across hospitals and payers at varying stages of implementation.

Representatives from 4 hospitals and 2 payers participated in focus group discussions. The doula programs were categorized as Anticipated, Initial and Advanced implementation status. Coding and thematic analysis were conducted using a deductive application of the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research.

There were 20 participants across 5 focus group discussions. Participants were mostly female, and nearly all had worked at their organization for at least 2 years. Salient themes shared across participants included valuing internal outcome data or peer reviewed literature to support doula care as well as anecdotal stories; reality of the resource-intensive nature of doula care implementation that goes beyond funding for doulas; and both the need for individual champions for change, such as midwives, and a supportive organizational culture that values health equity.

The findings of this study highlight 3 contextual aspects that should be considered when implementing doula programs. These recommendations include: (1) use of a combination of research evidence and anecdotes when eliciting stakeholder support; (2) consideration of resources beyond funding such as program implementation support; (3) critical evaluation of organizational culture as a primary driver influencing the implementation of doula care. The future of the doula workforce in United States hospitals rests on the crux of intentional buy-in from hospital administration and clinical providers as well as the availability of requisite resources.

## Abstract

Implementation of doula programs with multi-level stakeholders can be resource-intensive and are more likely to be successful when including personal anecdotes of positive collaborations with doulas along with current evidence on the efficacy of doula support. Hospitals, payers, and implementers should consider using both data and anecdotes to gain support, being cognizant of the resources needed for this collaboration.

## INTRODUCTION

The unacceptably high and inequitable rates of pregnancy-related deaths in the United States continue to persist, with the maternal mortality rate for non-Hispanic Black women at 69.9 deaths per 100,000 live births, versus 26.6 deaths per 100,000 live births for White women.1 In Massachusetts, publicly-insured women are 3 times as likely to die from pregnancy-related causes and have higher rates of maternal morbidities, as compared to privately-insured women.2 A systematic review of 2 decades of research on reducing maternal mortality showed that doula care improved birth outcomes when compared with hospital-based interventions, such as bundle implementation.3

Doulas are trained, non-medical providers who provide emotional, informational, and physical support during pregnancy, labor, and the postpartum period.4 Community doulas provide the same foundational support and additional visits and navigation at low or no cost and often share the same race, culture, or primary language as their clients.4 Doulas can anchor their work within hospital programs, nonprofit organizations, and as small businesses in their communities. Doula care can be part of team-based solutions to controlling chronic illnesses, such as hypertension.5 This may be meaningful since the leading causes of maternal mortality for non-Hispanic Black women is hypertensive diseases.6

Despite the known benefits of doula care, particularly for non-Hispanic Black women,7 doula support is underutilized.8 Publicly-insured women are 50% less likely to be aware of doulas than privately-insured women.9 However, Medicaid funding for doula care is being implemented or considered in several US states,10 with the intent to increase access to doulas by overcoming cost barriers.11,12 Despite increased access, the challenging task of implementation remains. Identifying both implementation barriers and solutions is important as the demand for doula care increases.13

Midwives, in particular, have played a critical role in championing maternity care innovations, such as newborn skin-to-skin contact after cesarean birth.14 Midwifery-led hospital-based models of doula care that focus on workflows and integration help to increase access to doula care, reduce health disparities, and contribute to doula care sustainability.15 Midwives remain uniquely positioned to facilitate multistakeholder collaboration, while upholding the values of reproductive justice,12 which is essential for non-Hispanic Black women’s outcomes.16

Given these policy implications and potential impact on racial inequities, the study of implementing community-based doula care holds value. This paper aims to understand doula program implementation within hospitals and payers using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research to identify barriers and facilitators at varying stages of implementation.17

## METHODS

This study features qualitative data collected as part of the third aim of a larger parent study18, which examined maternal safety bundles from the Alliance on Innovation in Maternal Health. This parent study included the bundle on the Reduction of Peripartum Racial/Ethnic Disparities, as well as how doulas affect clinical outcomes, such as cesarean birth rates among Black birthing individuals.19 For this study, qualitative methods were chosen, because we wanted to understand how doula implementation worked (or did not work) among participating hospitals, payers, and doulas within the parent study. Focus groups, as opposed to individual interviews, were chosen because doulas and program implementers tend to confide in one another and reflect on their experiences in doing this work. The focus group discussion facilitator used a semi-structured interview guide (see Table 1) developed using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research Interview Guide Tool.20 Questions were chosen for their likelihood of yielding modifiable barriers and facilitators to doula care implementation as well as relevance to the stage of implementation for each payer, doula program, or hospital (referred to hereafter as “organizations”) studied. Quality Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research were used to ensure methodological transparency (Supplementary Table S1).21

### Setting and Participants

Participants were eligible if they were directly involved in doula care implementation at any of the 4 hospitals that collaborated on the parent study (Table 2). To recruit for focus groups, each study hospital team leader invited participants whom they believed were essential to the implementation of doula care at their hospital. The resulting groups included a mix of clinical leadership (obstetricians, midwives, and nurses), administrative supporters, and in some cases, payers who have a doula care benefit for members with specific public plans.

Two of the hospitals have had a doula program for at least 3 or more years. One payer had implemented a doula care benefit for 3 years, which included prenatal and postpartum visits and labor and delivery support. A second payer began offering prenatal and postpartum visits from doulas 7 years ago and added labor and delivery support 1 year ago (Table 3). All of the hospitals except Hospital 4 have fully funded doula programs, either through the hospital’s operating budget or doula services are reimbursed by the payer whose plan members deliver at that site. The participants were mostly female, and nearly all had worked at their organization for at least 2 years (Table 4).

### Data Collection

We conducted 5 focus group discussions, held virtually, with between 3 and 5 participants in each group (n=20) lasting between 75 and 90 minutes per focus group discussion. Each hospital participated in its own focus group discussion. One payer joined the hospital focus group discussion where most of their members deliver, and the other payer opted to have a standalone discussion. Discussions were audio-recorded using Zoom and transcribed using www.rev.com. All focus group discussions took place in July 2021. Participants were given a $40 gift card for their participation using funding from the parent study.

### Rigor and Reflexivity

Co-authors engaged in reflexivity, which is the notion that all researchers bring their own experiences, expertise, and biases to their work.22,23,24 HAO facilitated the focus group discussions, created the initial codebook, coded the data, participated in thematic analysis, and identifies as a Black/African American female epidemiologist and doctoral student. TJR observed and assisted with data collection, coded the data, participated in thematic analysis, and identifies as a medical student and a Black/African American female. CBS served as a qualitative analyst, engaged in thematic development, and identifies as a maternal health services researcher and a white woman. CG co-designed the interview guide, led the qualitative analysis team, participated in thematic analysis, and identifies as a white female, a birth doula, and an advocate for the reimbursement of doulas. EL is a white female and implementation scientist who has given birth twice, co-designed the study and interview guide, and contributed to the thematic analysis. NAO serves as the principal investigator of the parent study, contributed to the writing of the manuscript, and identifies as a Black woman.

### Ethical Considerations

The study received approval from The Social Behavioral & Educational Research Institutional Review Board at Tufts University. All focus group participants provided verbal consent prior to starting the recording of the discussion. Written consent was waived.

### Data Analysis

Two independent coders began the initial coding and compilation of the codebook using NVivo qualitative software (QSR International Pty Ltd. Version 12, 2018). Using the first transcript, codes were mapped onto the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research framework using a deductive coding approach. Initial codes were then used by the second coder to code the first transcript. A third coder joined the research team after the initial codebook development. Cohen’s kappa coefficients were calculated to assess inter-rater reliability with each additional transcript coded.14 Initial kappa coefficients fell in the range of 0.5–0.71. The 3 coders engaged in an iterative process of coding, checking agreement, and discussing excerpts whenever kappa coefficients were below 0.70, further refining the codebook.

Themes were generated by examining both the number of subsequent codes and references for each Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research construct. Within salient constructs of the framework, excerpts were examined for notable differences and similarities across categories of implementation.

## RESULTS

Five themes emerged during analysis: (1)value of strength of evidence for stakeholder buy-in; (2)the unique value of doula care; (3) doula care as a resource-intensive intervention; (4) organizational culture contributes to doula implementation success; (5) champions needed, unique to each context.

### Theme 1: Value of Strength of Evidence for Stakeholder Buy-In

Midwives, nurses, department chairs, and high-level administration spoke of the value of peer-reviewed literature findings being necessary for stakeholder buy-in. The importance of existing peer-reviewed research showing doula care as an effective intervention was mentioned by Hospitals 2 and 4 as well as Payer 2. Research showing the impact of doula care on a Medicaid population came up in Hospitals 2 and 4:

“If it is steeped in something that’s published and vetted, for me, that has meaning [be]cause that’s really my standard go-to first beyond the anecdotal experiences, which also come in both from the patients and from the doulas.” (Hospital 4)

The value of data, which show that doula care can lower healthcare costs or provide a return on investment came up from Hospital 1 and Payer 2:

“You need to prove to the practices, to the Accountable Care Organizations that it’s worth having…We all feel the emotional need, the emotional support, but when it comes down to who’s going to pay for it…people need to see that there’s a return on investment.” (Payer 2)

Hospital 1 participants valued internal clinical data on outcomes such as nulliparity, term, singleton, and vertex cesarean birth rates. Survey data on patient or member satisfaction with doula care came up in Hospitals 1 and 4 and Payer 2. Anecdotal data, stories of how a doula impacted a particular family, were influential in gaining stakeholder buy-in according to Hospitals 1 and 4 and Payer 2.

### Theme 2: The Unique Value of Doula Care

All participants agreed that there were similarities between the scope of work of doulas and community health workers, which was the most frequently named related profession. Community health workers are frontline public health workers and trusted members of their communities whose scope of work includes navigation to health and social services, outreach, health education, advocacy, and social support.25 Participants noted that both community health workers and doulas are not in clinical roles but help navigate patients towards resources addressing social determinants of health, defined as the conditions in which people live that contribute to health risks and outcomes.26 While doulas share some overlap in scope with community health workers, all organizations stated that the role of the doula is distinct.

For example, participants from Hospitals 1 and 2 reported that doulas have a unique role in working with clients during pregnancy, birth, and postpartum, with specialized training to provide support during these 3 periods. Doulas focus on trust, intimacy, emotional support “holding space,” being a witness to the care the client receives and emphasizing empowerment and reflection on the care and birth experiences.

“I’m [doula] actually giving her [client] time to understand what’s going on. A lot of times [the clients] don’t really get the risks, benefits, and then information as they need it on their level. So, with me being there, that’s the only different aspect that is [there] and that the client appreciates. I believe when I leave a birth, the doctor, as well as the midwife, appreciates it, too, because they have time to go visit their other client while I’m explaining it more in depth with the client the procedure done or what medication needs to be done.” (Hospital 4)

Furthermore, the doula’s role is to be available for support to their clients 24 hours a day,7 days a week. Doulas’ ability to help mitigate birth trauma was brought up by Hospitals 1 and 3. Participants from 2 organizations (Hospital 1 and Payer 2) agreed that while the roles are both similar and unique, the specific needs of the birthing person should determine the type of support offered.

### Theme 3: Doula Care as a Resource Intensive Intervention

All participants agreed that cost was a challenge in providing doula care, noting that a doula program is very resource-intensive to implement. Participants noted that cost constraints made doulas a limited resource, doula programs required consistent support staff, and doulas must be paid a livable wage. Participants from Hospitals 3 and 4 described doula care as a limited resource to spread among high-need populations, resulting in lack of availability to [all of] those who could potentially benefit from doula support:

“Not every birthing person who could benefit from [our doula program] gets one. And I think it just speaks to the program being more resource intensive than some of the other programs… I don’t see that as a challenge, but I think it’s a challenge if you’re a program administrator trying to figure out how we’re going to staff and fund this thing.” (Hospital 1)

Participants reported the need for coordinators (Hospitals 1 and 2), managers (Hospital 1), supervisors (Hospital 2), and time for other supportive staff (Hospital 1) who may navigate patients into the doula program. Even if a doula program was fully funded, there were delays in initiating implementation due to challenges with nursing shortages (Hospital 3). Participants from Hospitals 1 and 4 reported that implementation can be a particular challenge when there is staff turnover. Additionally, participants from Hospitals 1 and 2 and Payer 2 discussed emotional costs related to implementation. Since doulas serve high-need populations, the risk of burnout is high, and there is often not enough time for doulas to process their own experiences.

“It’s really energy taxing to be on call 24/7, to be holding really intense emotional space for people, to try to navigate and coordinate having multiple patients at once that there just needs to be more funding to support the aftercare that doulas need themselves.” (Hospital 1)

Financial limitations to supporting doulas were identified. Participants from hospital 2 noted that doulas must be paid a livable wage to demonstrate the value of their work. Participants from Hospital 1 spoke of having to scale back some of the doula services due to organizational budget fluctuations.

### Theme 4: Organizational Culture Contributes to Doula Implementation Success

All participants spoke about organizational culture as a facilitator or barrier to the successful implementation of doula care. Several participants (Hospitals 1, 3, and 4) spoke of the mission-driven nature of their organization as a facilitator to implementation and buy-in among leadership, which added to the widespread value of working towards health equity.

“I’ve been at [redacted] for over 30 years, and one of the hallmarks of the culture… is that we take care of each patient the way we would want our own family member to be cared for. And so that means giving people all the information that we can give them to make decisions, collaborative decision-making, respect for differences of opinions… I strive to do that every day, and I think it’s something that we as a group do strive to do.” (Hospital 3)

Conversely, participants from Hospital 1 and 4 spoke of their organization being more “medical-driven” (Hospital 1) or “interventional,” or not supportive of “physiologic birth” and “patient autonomy” (Hospital 4) as a barrier to overcome.

Other participants reported buy-in for doulas was driven by providers’ acceptance of a doula program (Hospitals 1 and 2), and several participants noted buy-in being driven by nurses (Hospitals 2 and 4).

### Theme 5: Champions Needed, Unique to Each Context

All participants noted there must be buy-in for the doula program at all clinical and administrative levels, yet when it came to championing the implementation of doula care, participants differed in who they felt was most influential.

“There are two things that need to happen. One is getting leadership on board, [because] if you don’t have leadership on board, you’re not going anywhere. But that may not be sufficient, because you also need a champion…and it can’t be someone who just likes to shout. It has to be someone that people respect.” (Hospital 4)

Participants noted that providers (physicians and midwives) influence patients with their opinions and advice, championing the uptake of doula care.

“It does help as far as engaging our [population], if the health centers or their providers are on board with the program because then it’s not just us telling them about this program that we’re offering.” (Hospital 3, Payer 2)

Obstetric department leadership has decision-making authority in determining what interventions to take on (Hospitals 1–4). Moreover, quality and safety must ensure programs do not pose a threat to patients (Hospital 4), and the Development Office supports the doula programs by raising funds and aligning it with the mission-driven culture (Hospital 1). Senior administration among payers, such as the Medicaid or Medical Directors and top health plan executives value the financial return on investment (Payers 1 and 2).

“Our medical director was acting as the chief medical officer. [They were] our big champions. [They] believed in the program [and] thought it should be available to everybody, not just free to public plans, but it should be really open to any member who wants it across lines of business.” (Payer 2)

Participants also identified nurses, particularly nursing leadership, as a key group to engage, as nurses often execute upper-level administrative decisions downstream, while juggling many competing priorities (Hospitals 1, 2 and 4).

“One of the problems you get into when you have that is that’s when you get, like, the nurses and staff rebelling, because things are being dumped on them that they haven’t bought into.” (Hospital 2)

## DISCUSSION

In this study, participants from hospitals, payers, and doula programs described the implementation context for programs from anticipated through advanced implementation.

Largely, there were similarities across sites in terms of the themes, which arose from the data in this study. There were, however, some nuances in how sites described evidence needed for buy-in. Some emphasized peer-reviewed literature, while participants from Hospital 1 noted organizational internal satisfaction data. The value of anecdotal data or personal stories about experiences with doulas aligns with previous work showing that clinicians’ own experiences with doulas heavily influence their perceptions,27 though more research is needed on this topic.28 The Racial Inequities in Maternal Health Commission29 in Massachusetts serves as an example of soliciting stories about doula care through the use of community listening sessions.30

Providing evidence, however, is not sufficient for successful implementation. Participants discussed the need for both a supportive organizational culture and champions for change. Evidence on organizational culture around health inequities, which may improve the implementation context for doula support, is still emerging.31 Implementing a doula program takes time for the ideas and buy-in to spread to various levels of stakeholders. While clinical or administrative leadership must be on board, champions, such as midwives, nurses, and physicians are imperative. Finally, the economic burden of administrative and clinical time as well as equitable and fair wages for doula work must be considered. A 2023 initiative through Health Connect One helps to make this consideration easier by using the “Doula FAST” tool to project a budget for implementation and maintenance of a doula program.32

### Implications for Policy and Practice

In the wider context, Medicaid reimbursement for doula care continues to be a nationwide policy discussion, with many states opting to pass legislation to ensure coverage of doula services10 thus improving access.12 However, this study demonstrates that access does not necessarily facilitate implementation. For example, Hospital 3 had funding from a payer for a doula program but did not have staffing resources for coordination, which delayed implementation. Likewise, Hospital 4 had departmental support for a doula program, however still required a separate funding source. Moreover, Medicaid reimbursement alone is unlikely to sufficiently cover these administrative costs. Billing for doula services is new in many states with uncertainty as to actual reimbursement collections compared to what is billed. Even with financial support,33 doula care can be resource intensive. However, multiple studies have identified the lower healthcare costs associated with doula programs;34,35 other studies have demonstrated improvement in clinical outcomes.36 More research is needed that evaluates costs and benefits while taking into account other outcomes that are not as easily quantifiable in the long term, such as patient satisfaction and returning to the organization for a subsequent birth.

All the organizations in this study discussed the value of reducing health inequities, suggesting its salience as a potential facilitator. However, employing doulas to achieve health equity may contribute to burnout. The value of racial concordance between doulas and their clients37 must also consider the unique experience of Black doulas who experience stigma16 and are witnesses to their clients’ inequitable care, a reality these data confirm.38 Moreover, racial concordance does not necessarily address cultural concordance,38 and cultural humility is critical in doula-client relationships.39

Similarly, an interventional culture was seen as a barrier to implementation among participants. Midwives have expertise in supporting physiological birth and are natural champions for successful implementation.40 Health systems that have yet to embrace (or prioritize) a culture of health equity will likely require greater efforts shifting organizational culture and will require strategies that foster change.41 This could include policy-level strategies, such as requiring health systems to support doulas, and more local strategies, such as providing education on the impact of doulas. Ongoing evidence demonstrating the impact of doulas on health disparities and outcomes will be key.42,43

### Strengths and Limitations

This study has several strengths. First, participants represented multiple programs, ranging in different stages of implementation. This intentional inclusion of a variety of perspectives provides a robust examination of doula implementation in hospital systems and a comparison of the context for doula implementation across stakeholders and stages. Specifically, including the voices of payers in the current study adds novel context to the work and provides opportunities for researchers and doulas alike to consider new ways of partnering with payers to improve patient care. Second, the researchers were reflexive at each stage of the research process. Finally, these data add to the parent study by triangulating the use of large longitudinal outcome datasets with quality improvement methods (bundles) and a community-driven intervention (doulas). This combination of epidemiological, clinical, and community-driven angles to reduce maternal health inequities adds further weight to previous systematic reviews.3

This study also has several limitations. First, participants representing all providers and payers were within the same state, and results may not be transferable to other parts of the country. Second, the participants represented the existing structure of the participating organizations and are thus reflective of this context. Third, 2 authors were employed at two of the organizations included in the study, possibly causing hesitation among participants in freely discussing program limitations. However, neither author was present in the focus group discussion, limiting the likelihood of significant bias. Finally, the presence of supervisors in one of the groups may have also resulted in reluctance to respond truthfully regarding barriers to implementation.

## CONCLUSION

The benefits of doulas are emphasized from both an organizational and provider perspective in this study. Opportunities exist for strengthening the healthcare system to ensure that all birthing people have access to doula care. The future of the doula workforce in US hospitals is predicated on having consistent buy-in from hospital administration and clinical providers, as well as requisite financial and staffing resources. Midwives, who often work alongside doulas and who serve as champions of doula care, are crucial for increasing organizational buy-in for health equity programs, like doulas. The work of doulas is inherently connected to organizational culture, particularly a culture, which values health equity for all. As the United States continues to work towards the elimination of maternal health inequities as experienced by Black birthing individuals, successful implementation of doula programs will be a critical discussion both among healthcare institutions and the national policy arena.
